key_strategies: Marshall Plan rebuilds Western Europe to stabilize politics and markets.
notable_policies_events: Permanent garrisons in Europe/Asia under NATO umbrella

key_strategies: Alliances + covert action to counter communism.
Early export-control coordination and military-industrial scaling.
notable_policies_events: Guatemala 1954 (Operation PBSUCCESS): paramilitary, air ops, propaganda

key_strategies: Flexible response; tech/space signaling; foreign aid competition in Global South.
notable_policies_events: Crisis management approach; continued NATO investment

key_strategies: Vietnam commitment; continued use of Bretton Woods tools.
Dollar off gold; manage oil shock via Saudi ties; détente with USSR/PRC.
notable_policies_events: 1971 end of gold convertibility; 1973–74 oil shock; 1974 US–Saudi Joint Commission
Institutionalization of US–Saudi commissions and recycling mechanisms
Persian Gulf identified as vital interest

key_strategies: Defense-tech buildup; market liberalization within US-led order.
Coalition warfare + sanctions to police order in Gulf War.
notable_policies_events: 1991 Gulf War; UN-backed sanctions and force projection

key_strategies: NATO enlargement, globalization, and rise of US tech platforms.
Post-9/11 wars; sanctions expansion; SWIFT data scrutiny to counter terror finance.
notable_policies_events: Afghanistan and Iraq wars; intensified terror finance controls

key_strategies: Pivot to Asia; drones/cyber; Iran sanctions leading to JCPOA.
notable_policies_events: Sanctions architecture on Iran tightened pre-JCPOA (2015)

key_strategies: Trade/tech coercion versus China; tariff weaponization; entity-list actions.
Industrial policy at home (CHIPS/IRA) and export controls abroad (2022–24).
Alliance repair; AUKUS/Quad; sanctions & SWIFT against Russia (2022).
notable_policies_events: Oct 7, 2022 BIS rule; Oct 2023 updates; 2024 refinements
AUKUS (2021) and revived Quad; Russia sanctions & SWIFT bans (2022)

key_strategies: Early-term recalibration of tech controls/industrial subsidies and alliance burden-sharing under review.

bretton_woods_imf_world_bank.description: Post-1944 monetary order with IMF and World Bank enabling reconstruction, balance-of-payments support, and US agenda-setting power.

dollar_centrality_petrodollar_practice.description: Post-1971 dollar dominance sustained by liquidity, Treasury markets, and US–Saudi economic/security cooperation (1974 Joint Commission), not a formal dollar-only oil treaty.

sanctions_payments_plumbing.description: OFAC sanctions and selective SWIFT disconnections (Iran 2012, Russia 2022) leverage network effects of the dollar; encourage partial alternatives (SPFS/CIPS).

semiconductor_rules_2022_2024.description: BIS rules restrict advanced AI chips, equipment, and US-person support; widened in 2023–24; effectiveness tied to allied alignment (Japan/Netherlands).

overseas_bases.description: Forward presence for deterrence/logistics. Official counts acknowledge ~128 bases in ≥51 countries; broader civil tallies cite ~750 sites depending on definitions.

alliances.description: NATO creation and successive enlargements; Indo-Pacific relies on bilateral treaties and newer minilateral frameworks (Quad, AUKUS).

grand_strategy_context.description: US-led liberal order (open markets, alliances, institutions) with debates over primacy vs. restraint across administrations.

interaction_patterns.insight: Dollar scale/liquidity and SWIFT access make sanctions potent but also catalyze alternative rails (SPFS/CIPS) with repeated use.
Performance-threshold controls plus U.S.-person rules constrain AI compute; long-run effectiveness depends on allied sync and China’s indigenization timeline.
Forward basing underwrites deterrence, export-control enforcement, and sanctions; counts differ by methodology but show enduring Europe/Indo-Pacific concentration.

strategies_effectiveness.effectiveness: Historically decisive in WWII cases; mixed and costly in recent decades
High leverage via dollar/SWIFT network; catalyzes workarounds over time
High for policy synchronization and deterrence
Effective at chokepoints; depends on allied alignment

latin_america.reason: Hemispheric primacy rooted in the Monroe Doctrine and its evolution into a justification for frequent intervention to secure a U.S.-led order in the Western Hemisphere.

Domestic security spillovers: reduce mass migration, neutralize drug cartels and transnational crime, prevent hostile ownership of critical assets, and secure nearby strategic locations ("front yard" framing).
Countering extra‑hemispheric rivals (China, Russia) expanding influence and investments in Latin America.
Regime change / anti‑communism during the Cold War and after (e.g., Guatemala 1954; Chile 1973) using sanctions, covert action, and direct/multilateral force.
Protection of U.S. commercial interests and energy/resource access through embargoes, sanctions, and political pressure (e.g., Cuba, Venezuela).

asia_pacific.reason: Protect global trade routes and supply chains; maintain access to key strategic locations, sea lanes, and basing/overflight rights.
Counterbalance the rise of China via alliances and minilateral frameworks (AUKUS, Quad) and military-technological cooperation.
Counterterrorism and denial of safe havens (post‑9/11) leading to Afghanistan operations and broader War on Terror.
Preserve regional stability through forward presence and alliance commitments (Japan, ROK, Philippines, Australia).

comparison_latin_america_vs_asia.overview: Contrasting U.S. motives, tools, and mechanisms across regions.

primary_drivers: Hemispheric primacy and Monroe Doctrine legacies (Keep external powers out; justify interventions).
Internal U.S. security concerns (migration, narco‑crime) and regime alignment near U.S. borders.
Countering China/Russia’s influence and protecting U.S. commercial/energy interests.
typical_mechanisms: Covert action, support for coups or friendly regimes (e.g., Guatemala 1954; Chile 1973).
Limited/direct interventions and maritime deployments in the Caribbean basin.

primary_drivers: Great‑power balancing—counter China; sustain rules‑based order via alliances and minilaterals.
Protection of global supply chains and critical sea lanes.
Counterterrorism and denial of safe havens (post‑9/11).
typical_mechanisms: Major combat operations/occupations (Japan 1945–52; Korea; Vietnam; Afghanistan; Iraq).
Defense treaties and minilateral pacts (U.S.–Japan, U.S.–ROK, Philippines; AUKUS; Quad).
Export controls/tech alliances to constrain rival capabilities.

top_strategies.name: Sanctions & Financial Pressure
top_strategies.why: Proximity + dollar exposure + trade ties make sanctions and banking access pressure bite quickly; often yields concessions or regime strain.

top_strategies.name: Covert/Political Operations
top_strategies.why: Historically decisive in some cases (e.g., Guatemala 1954, Chile 1973), but reputational costs and regional backlash limit repeatability today.

top_strategies.name: Alliance/Security Leverage & Diplomatic Isolation
top_strategies.why: Hemispheric primacy/Monroe legacy and regional coalitions amplify pressure but face pushback from growing extra‑regional actors.

top_strategies.name: Major Combat / Occupation (historical)
top_strategies.why: Compelled surrender (Japan 1945), enabled constitutional redesign; but today’s costs/risks + nuclear/peer dynamics raise thresholds.

top_strategies.name: Alliances, Minilaterals & Access/Basing
top_strategies.why: Defense treaties (Japan/ROK/Philippines) + AUKUS/Quad synchronize policies and posture across the Indo‑Pacific.

top_strategies.name: Tech/Export Controls
top_strategies.why: BIS rules restrict advanced compute; effectiveness depends on allied alignment and evasion limits.

top_strategies.name: Sanctions
top_strategies.why: Impacts hinge on target’s dollar exposure and alternative networks (e.g., CIPS/SPFS) mitigating effects.

regions.region: Middle East / Islamic-majority states (subset of Asia/Africa)

top_strategies.name: Counterterrorism/Major Combat Operations
top_strategies.why: Taliban toppled (2001) but long insurgency; Iraq 2003 toppled Saddam but met prolonged insurgency and high costs.

top_strategies.name: Coalition Warfare & Sanctions
top_strategies.why: Gulf War expelled Iraq from Kuwait quickly; sanctions often extract concessions but can entrench regimes.

asia_interventions_timeline.summary: U.S. fought Filipino revolutionaries after annexation; American victory established U.S. rule; heavy civilian toll.
U.S.-led occupation transformed Japan’s political economy and security posture; ended with 1952 peace treaty.
U.S.-led UN Command intervened to defend South Korea; war ended in armistice and creation of DMZ.
Escalating U.S. advisory and combat role under Cold War containment; withdrawal completed by 1973.
U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait; cease-fire framework shaped 1990s sanctions/inspections.
Response to 9/11: toppled Taliban, long counterinsurgency; NATO/ISAF mission ended 2014; U.S. presence ended 2021.
U.S.-led invasion toppled Saddam; prolonged insurgency; withdrawal completed Dec 2011.

forced_surrenders.why: Defeat in the American Revolutionary War; Treaty of Paris recognized U.S. independence.
Unconditional surrender of Nazi Germany at the end of WWII.
Unconditional surrender after atomic bombings and Soviet entry into the war.
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: Foreign Minister Mamoru Shigemitsu and Gen. Yoshijiro Umezu

forced_surrenders.why: Defeat in the Mexican–American War; Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: José Bernardo Couto, Miguel de Atristain, Luis Gonzaga Cuevas (Mexico); Nicholas Trist (U.S.)

forced_surrenders.why: Defeat in the Spanish–American War; Treaty of Paris (1898).
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: Eugenio Montero Ríos, Buenaventura de Abarzuza, José de Garnica, Wenceslao Ramírez de Villa-Urrutia, Rafael Cerero (Spain); William R. Day and others (U.S.)

forced_surrenders.why: Collapse of Mussolini’s government; Italy accepted unconditional armistice with Allies.
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: General Giuseppe Castellano (Italy); General Walter Bedell Smith (Allies)

forced_surrenders.why: Bulgarian military/political collapse; accepted Allied armistice terms.
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: P. Stainov, D. Terpeshev, N. Petkov, P. Stoyanov (Bulgaria); Lt. Gen. James Gammell, Marshal F.I. Tolbukhin (Allies)

forced_surrenders.why: Military defeat and encirclement by Soviet forces; Hungary accepted Allied terms.
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: Gyöngyosi János, Vörös János, Balogh István (Hungary); Marshal K.E. Voroshilov (Allies)

forced_surrenders.why: King Michael's coup; Romania ceased hostilities and surrendered to the Allies.
forced_surrenders.who_signed_for_opponent: Lucrețiu Pătrășcanu, Gen. D. Dămăceanu, Prince Știrbey, G. Popp (Romania); Marshal R.Y. Malinovski (Allies)

additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.why: Military defeat in WWI; Armistice of Mudros ended Ottoman participation in the war.
additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.who_signed_for_opponent: Rauf Bey (Ottoman Empire); Admiral Gough-Calthorpe (Great Britain for Allies)

additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.why: Austria had been annexed by Nazi Germany (Anschluss, 1938); thus surrendered implicitly with Germany.
additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.who_signed_for_opponent: German High Command (Austria had no separate delegation).

additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.country: German Forces in Northern Italy and Western Austria
additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.why: Operation Sunrise led to German surrender of nearly 1 million troops in Italy and Austria.
additional_forced_surrenders_not_directl.who_signed_for_opponent: Gen. von Vietinghoff (Germany); Lt. Gen. Morgan for Field Marshal Harold Alexander (Allies)
